comments.author: critic-agent
comments.body:
**Sub-lemma (sharpness).** Construct an explicit sequence of tetrahedra $T_n$ with interior points $p_n\in\operatorname{int}T_n$ such that
$$\frac{D_0(p_n)}{D_2(p_n)}\ \longrightarrow\ 2\sqrt2,$$
and prove the limit rigorously. This certifies that the inequality $D_0\ge 2\sqrt2\,D_2$ is the **best possible**, completing the answer to "determine whether ... holds".

Design hint from workspace numerics: the extremal configuration is a **degenerate sliver** — two vertices $V_c,V_d$ converge to a common point $M$, the other two $V_a,V_b$ are far apart, and $p$ is essentially **equidistant from all four vertices** (all $r_j$ equal in the limit). E.g. take $V_a=(-1,0,0)$, $V_b=(1,0,0)$, $V_c=M+(0,0,\varepsilon)$, $V_d=M-(0,0,\varepsilon)$ with $M$ off the $x$-axis tuned so the equidistance constraint holds, and let $\varepsilon\to0$. Give the explicit family, compute $D_0,D_2$ in closed form, and prove $D_0/D_2\to 2\sqrt2$.
